claim: Odors typically activate multiple olfactory receptor neuron (ORN) classes and are therefore represented by the patterns of active ORNs.
source: Odors typically activate multiple olfactory receptor neuron (ORN) classes and are therefore represented by the patterns of active ORNs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Hallem et al., 2004; Malnic et al., 1999).

claim: In response to similarly attractive odors, flies modulate their locomotion differently.
source: In this arena, in response to similarly attractive odors, flies modulate their locomotion differently implying that odors have a more diverse effect on locomotion than was anticipated.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data comparing ACV and 2-butanone responses.

claim: In response to odors, flies modulate a surprisingly large number of motor parameters.
source: First, in response to odors, flies modulate a surprisingly large number of motor parameters.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the identification of 17 motor parameters that are modulated by odors.

claim: Similarly attractive odors elicit changes in different motor programs.
source: Second, similarly attractive odors elicit changes in different motor programs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through comparison of ACV2 and BUN3 responses.

claim: Different ORN classes modulate different subset of motor parameters.
source: Third, different ORN classes modulate different subset of motor parameters.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experiments activating specific ORN classes with low concentrations of odors.

claim: Individual ORNs express only one or few ORs in phylogenetically diverse species.
source: In phylogenetically diverse species, individual ORNs express only one or few ORs (Buck and Axel, 1991; Su et al., 2009) which largely determine their response specificity; thus ORNs can be classified into a discrete number of classes (Vosshall et al., 1999; Vosshall et al., 2000; Clyne et al., 1999; Clyne et al., 1999) according to the OR gene they express.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Each odor activates multiple ORN classes and is represented by an ensemble of active ORN classes.
source: Each odor activates multiple ORN classes and is represented by an ensemble of active ORN classes (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Hallem et al., 2004; Malnic et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Only a minority of chemical communication occurs through the detection of rare, highly-specialized chemicals by a single ORN class.
source: Recent work has shown that only a minority of chemical communication occurs through the detection of rare, highly-specialized chemicals by a single ORN class (Kaissling, 1996; Dorries et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most chemical communication involves integration of signals from multiple ORN classes.
source: Most chemical communication involves integration of signals from multiple ORN classes (Christensen and Sorensen, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The behavioral arena creates a sharp interface between a central zone of constant odor concentration and a surrounding no-odor zone.
source: A push-pull arrangement whereby air is pushed into the arena via an inlet tube and pulled through the arena by vacuum creates a sharp interface between a central zone of constant odor concentration (i.e. the odor-zone) and a surrounding no-odor zone.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus design.

claim: Smoke introduced through the inlet tube was confined to the odor-zone.
source: To demonstrate that the odor is limited to the odor-zone, we performed smoke visualization, and found that smoke introduced through the inlet tube was confined to the odor-zone, implying that odor from the inlet tube should also be limited to the odor-zone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by smoke visualization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The odor concentration decreases to less than 10% of its peak 3 mm away from the boundary of the nominal odor-zone.
source: We estimate that the odor concentration decreases to less than 10% of its peak 3 mm away from the boundary of the nominal odor-zone (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on EAG measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Flies spend 2.5-fold more time inside the odor-zone in the presence of apple cider vinegar than during the control period.
source: In the presence of apple cider vinegar (ACV), a strong attractant, flies spend 2.5-fold more time inside the odor-zone (Figure 1F) than during the control period.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 2-butanone was strongly attractive to the fly.
source: In an initial screen for attractive odors, using fractional time spent inside as the metric for quantifying attraction, we found that 2-butanone was strongly attractive to the fly (Figure 1H, statistical test for attraction shown in Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1H and statistical tests in Figure 4.

claim: Flies decrease their speed when they enter the odor-zone in the presence of ACV0 but not in the presence of BUN3.
source: Flies decrease their speed when they enter the odor-zone in the presence of ACV0 but not in the presence of BUN3 (Figure 2A ; also see Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: As the flies exit the odor-zone there is an increase in speed in the presence of ACV0 but not in the presence of BUN3.
source: Conversely, as the flies exit the odor-zone there is an increase in speed in the presence of ACV0 but not in the presence of BUN3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 2B.

claim: In the presence of either ACV0 or BUN3, the long stops are largely abolished, and the median stop is only 0.3 s long.
source: In the presence of either odor, the long stops are largely abolished, and the median stop is only 0.3 s long (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of stop duration shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The run duration and speed during runs are only modulated in the presence of ACV0.
source: However, the run duration (Figure 2E, median 1.0 s) and speed during runs (Figure 2F, median speed decreased from 0.57 cm/s to 0.18 cm/s) are only modulated in the presence of ACV0.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: In the presence of ACV0, flies make sharp turns at the border between the odor and no-odor zone.
source: In the presence of ACV0, flies make sharp turns (see Materials and methods for our definition) at the border between the odor and no-odor zone (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: In the presence of BUN3, there is an overall increase in the frequency of turns in the presence of odor but the increase does not strongly peak at the odor interface.
source: In the presence of BUN3, there is an overall increase in the frequency of turns in the presence of odor but the increase does not strongly peak at the odor interface.
evidence: This is based on analysis of turning behavior in response to BUN3.

claim: Apple cider vinegar at a concentration of 10-2 (ACV2) had a similar level of attractiveness as BUN3.
source: To test this idea, we performed behavioral experiments at 5 concentrations of apple cider vinegar and found that apple cider vinegar at a concentration of 10-2 (ACV2) had a similar level of attractiveness as BUN3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by attraction index measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Unlike their response to BUN3, flies decreased their speed upon entering the odor-zone in the presence of ACV2.
source: Unlike their response to BUN3, flies decreased their speed upon entering the odor-zone in the presence of ACV2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 3B.

claim: The increased rate of sharp turns at the odor border observed with ACV0 was still observed at the lower concentration of ACV (ACV2).
source: Moreover, the increased rate of sharp turns at the odor border observed with ACV0 was still observed at the lower concentration of ACV (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 3C.

claim: 17 parameters are all significantly modulated by ACV0 at p <0.05.
source: Out of the parameters we investigated, we found 17 parameters (Table 1) that are all significantly (p <0.05 in a rank sum test) modulated by ACV0.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral parameters.

claim: The linear correlation between the 17 parameters is small, suggesting that they are largely independent of each other.
source: We expected these parameters to be dependent on each other; and measured pairwise correlation to identify dependent parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Surprisingly, we found that the linear correlation between these 17 parameters is small, suggesting that they are largely independent of each other.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first principal component only captured about 25% of the variance in data and the first seven principal components together contribute 90% to the variance in the data.
source: Instead, we found that the first principal component only captured about 25% of the variance in data and the first seven principal components together contribute 90% to the variance in the data (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Along the first canonical variate, the fly's response to ACV0 and BUN3 is clearly separable.
source: Along the first canonical variate, the fly's response to ACV0 and BUN3 is clearly separable (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by canonical variate analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Less than 0.3% of randomized trials had medians greater than the original distribution for ACV0 vs BUN3 comparison.
source: The median distance between the randomly assigned ACV0 and BUN3 groups was larger than the median distance between the original groups in only 0.3% of the trials (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on permutation test results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ACV0 activates 7 ORN classes.
source: Out of these 36 ORN classes, we found that ACV0 activates 7 ORN classes (Figure 6A , see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is based on single sensillum recording experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ethyl acetate at concentrations below 10-6 only activates Or42b-ORNs.
source: We have previously shown that ethyl acetate at a concentration <10-6 only activates Or42b-ORNs33,34 and confirmed that the same is true under the exact stimulus conditions used in this study (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ethyl acetate at 10-8 (ETA8) does not elicit attraction.
source: In behavioral experiments, we found that ethyl acetate at 10-8 (ETA8) does not elicit attraction (Figure 6C, first panel).
evidence: This is based on behavioral experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ETA8 elicits increase in angular speed and decrease in run duration compared to the solvent control.
source: However, the lack of attraction does not imply a lack of behavioral response; we measured how ETA8 affects each of the 17 parameters and found that ETA8 elicits increase in angular speed and decrease in run duration compared to the solvent control (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral parameter analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both the increase in angular speed and decrease in run duration by ETA8 are abolished in the Or42b null mutant.
source: Moreover, both the increase in angular speed and decrease in run duration by ETA8 are abolished in the Or42b null mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experiments with Or42b mutants shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: 2-butanone at 10-5 dilution (BUN5) only strongly activates Or42a-ORNs.
source: To activate Or42a-ORNs alone, we used 10-5 dilution of 2-butanone (BUN5), a concentration at which it only strongly activates Or42a-ORNs (Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on prior literature (Olsen et al., 2010).

claim: BUN5 results in the modulation of a small number of motor parameters.
source: We found that BUN5 also results in the modulation of a small number of motor parameters (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on behavioral parameter analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: BUN5 affects angular speed inside the odor-zone but does not affect run duration; rather it causes a decrease in stop duration.
source: Like ETA8, BUN5 affects angular speed inside the odor-zone. But unlike ETA8, it does not affect run duration; rather it causes a decrease in stop duration.
evidence: This is based on behavioral parameter analysis.

claim: Or42b-ORNs are the most sensitive to ACV out of the 7 ORNs activated by ACV.
source: Moreover, we found that of the 7 ORNs activated by ACV, Or42b-ORNs are the most sensitive (see below).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Or42b-ORNs are the only ones strongly activated by ACV4.
source: EAG response to ACV4 is abolished in the Or42b-mutant implying that the Or42b-ORNs are the only ORNs strongly activated by ACV4.
evidence: This is based on EAG measurements in Or42b mutants.

claim: ACV4 activates Or42b-ORNs alone and does not elicit attraction.
source: ACV4 activates Or42b-ORNs alone and expectedly does not elicit attraction (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ACV4 affects the same two parameters as ETA8 - run duration and angular speed inside.
source: As in the case of ETA8 (Figure 6C) lack of attraction does not imply a lack of behavioral response; ACV4 affects the same two parameters as ETA8 - run duration and angular speed inside (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral parameter analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: ACV3 activates Or59b-ORNs in addition to Or42b-ORNs.
source: ACV3 activates Or59b-ORNs in addition to Or42b-ORNs.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: ACV3 modulates more motor parameters than ACV4.
source: Behaviorally, ACV3 modulates more motor parameters (Figure 7D); this is likely due to the activation of more ORN classes.
evidence: This is based on behavioral parameter analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: At ACV2 dilution, 10 parameters are affected and the behavior appears qualitatively similar to the fly's behavior to ACV0.
source: The number of parameters modulated increases further when the concentration is increased to ACV2. At this dilution, 10 parameters are affected (Figure 7E) and the behavior appears qualitatively similar to the fly's behavior to ACV0.
evidence: This is based on behavioral parameter analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Or42b-mutants were as attracted to ACV as control flies.
source: Or42b-mutants were as attracted to ACV as control flies (Figure 8B,E -attraction index panel, p >0.1 on a ranksum test); but some of the individual motor parameters were affected in the mutant.
evidence: This is based on behavioral experiments with Or42b mutants shown in Figures 8B and 8E.

claim: The mutant flies had a significantly sharper distribution at the odor border compared to control flies.
source: The mutant flies had a significantly sharper distribution at the odor border (Figure 8B, C).
evidence: This is based on radial density analysis shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: The change in run duration was significantly diminished in the Or42b mutants compared to the control flies.
source: The change in run duration was significantly diminished in the mutants compared to the control flies (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is based on run duration analysis shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: Only 3 parameters out of 17 investigated were affected in the Or42b mutants.
source: Overall, only 3 parameters out of 17 we investigated were affected in the mutants (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is based on comprehensive behavioral parameter analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Out of the 7 ORN classes activated by ACV0, 3 ORNs require a co-receptor, Ir8a.
source: Out of the 7 ORN classes activated by ACV0, 3 ORNs require a co-receptor, Ir8a.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of ORN receptor requirements.

claim: In the Ir8a mutant, 3 ORN classes are non-functional and only 4 ORN classes activated by ACV0 are functional.
source: In the Ir8a mutant (Abuin et al., 2011), these 3 ORN classes are non-functional and only 4 ORN classes activated by ACV0 are functional (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the Ir8a mutant phenotype and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The Ir8a mutant flies are still attracted to ACV0.
source: The Ir8a mutant flies are still attracted to ACV0 (Figure 9D, p <0.0001 for both control and mutant in a ranksum test); there is a small but statistically insignificant decrease in attraction to ACV0 in the mutants compared to the control flies.
evidence: This is based on behavioral experiments with Ir8a mutants shown in Figure 9D.

claim: There is a large change in the modulation of 5 motor parameters out of the 17 under study in Ir8a mutants.
source: However, there is a large change in the modulation of 5 motor parameters out of the 17 under study (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is based on behavioral parameter analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The immediate modulation of speed upon entering the odor-zone is completely abolished in the Ir8a mutant.
source: The most striking difference between the wild-type and mutant is that the immediate modulation of speed upon entering the odor-zone is completely abolished in the mutant (Figure 9B, p >0.1 in a ranksum test for the mutants).
evidence: This is based on speed analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Modulation of speed as the fly exits the odor-zone is also abolished in Ir8a mutants.
source: Similarly, modulation of speed as the fly exits the odor-zone is also abolished (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is based on speed analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Most of the parameters affected in the Ir8a mutants are those that, in control flies, are affected as the fly crosses into the odor-zone or are modulated inside the odor-zone.
source: Most of the parameters affected in the mutants are those that, in control flies, are affected as the fly crosses into the odor-zone or are modulated inside the odor-zone.
evidence: This is based on analysis of which parameters are affected in the mutant.

claim: The initial increase in the time spent inside is similar for both Ir8a mutant and control flies.
source: The initial increase in the time spent inside is similar for both the mutant and the control.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of time spent inside the odor-zone.

claim: The fractional time inside peaks faster in Ir8a mutants compared to control flies.
source: However, the fractional time inside peaks faster in mutants suggesting that both mutant and control flies find the odor efficiently but the control flies stay inside the odor-zone for longer.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of time spent inside the odor-zone.

claim: Time inside per transit was longer for the wild-type flies throughout the entire 3 min that the odor was on.
source: Time inside per transit was longer for the wild-type flies throughout the entire 3 min that the odor was on.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Time to return is similar for wild-type and Ir8a mutant genotypes.
source: Time to return is similar for the two genotypes.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The Ir8a-mutant flies dispersed from the odor source at a much faster rate than did the controls in the point source experiment.
source: The Ir8a-mutant flies also navigated rapidly to the odor. But, the mutant flies dispersed from the odor source at a much faster rate than did the controls (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is based on point source behavioral experiments shown in Figure 10E.

claim: In the control flies, but not in Ir8a mutant flies, speed decreased in bins closer to the odor source in the point source experiment.
source: We measured the mean speeds in 5 radial bins and found that in the control flies, but not in Ir8a mutant flies, speed decreased in bins closer to the odor source (Figure 10F).
evidence: This is based on speed analysis in the point source experiment shown in Figure 10F.

claim: Animals are endowed with large families of odorant receptors (ORs) that are expressed in olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and bind to odors.
source: To meet the challenges of detecting and discriminating between different olfactory cues, animals are endowed with large families of odorant receptors (ORs) (Spehr and Munger, 2009; Touhara and Vosshall, 2009) that are expressed in olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and bind to odors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: ORs largely determine the response specificity of ORNs.
source: In phylogenetically diverse species, individual ORNs express only one or few ORs (Buck and Axel, 1991; Su et al., 2009) which largely determine their response specificity
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.
